b7d522acdad578db2e351cd84aad9110b81459bc.summary: South Korea's National Police Agency warned that the North Korean groups Lazarus, Andariel and Kimsuky breached South Korean defense companies and their subcontractors to steal defense technology data. A special inspection between January 15 and February 16 found multiple firms compromised since late 2022 without knowing it. Reported access methods included exploiting poorly managed test network connection systems, using a stolen account from a maintenance company employee, and exploiting an email server flaw that allowed unauthenticated large file downloads. It persists through a Registry Run Key, logs keystrokes, accepts remote commands, spreads through USB autorun files, and injects malicious macros into Excel macro-enabled files. b76a490ed0318d173fd53a7c87ea84606de26c3a.summary: A joint 2017 report by Trend Micro and Europol's EC3 on ATM malware. It covers physical attacks, where criminals open the machine and load malware from USB or CD, and network attacks that enter through a bank's corporate network. Families discussed include Skimer, Ploutus, Padpin, GreenDispenser and Alice. Network cases include the 2016 Taiwan attack, Cobalt Strike, Anunak/Carbanak, Ripper and ATMitch. It also covers NeoPocket and the Suceful test tool. Perpetrator groups are discussed as likely Eastern European or Latin American, with attribution hedged throughout.

hedges: Although attribution is a thorny issue, the discussion is more about the overall landscape and the business models behind these attacks.
The origin country for VirusTotal submissions can be manipulated using a VPN service, so the actual origins of the Suceful tool remain inconclusive.
Only a DLL could be recovered for ATMitch, so the report may not have the complete picture and cannot make a final call on how the method works.
No official police reports exist for the Malaysia incident; the Padpin attribution is based on technical facts and is described as most likely.
The Cobalt Strike and Anunak/Carbanak attackers may or may not be the same; the report says it cannot contest the claims of the firms that investigated.
Due to the public unavailability of the malware samples found on the Cobalt Strike-era ATMs, no additional analysis could be performed.
